results.title: My 140 reused passwords finally came back to bite me. Here’s how I fixed it
results.author: Megan Ellis
results.content:
My 140 reused passwords finally came back to bite me. Here's how I fixed it
Aug 1, 2026 — 6:00 AM ET
It’s famous online security lore that you shouldn’t reuse the same password across multiple accounts. But once upon a time, I was a naïve student who liberally ignored this rule, placing far too much trust in the companies that held my data.
Fast forward to 2026, and those bad habits have come back to bite an older and wiser version of myself. While I have long since stopped reusing passwords, the Ghost of Passwords Past decided to visit me when I was notified that my data had been exposed in a breach. And it ended up affecting a lot more than I expected.
Do you ever reuse your passwords for more than one account?
How did I even reuse the same password 140 times?
While I was aware that I’d used the password many times in the past, I hadn’t realized just how much. It was somewhat of a holy grail at the time: a secure password with random letters and characters — as well as one that I actually remembered.
At the time, password managers weren’t as ubiquitous as they are now. Chrome only introduced a built-in password manager around 2015, and it only started generating passwords in 2018. I had started using this password in 2009. These were the days of adding every game and quiz you could on Facebook (not realizing they were harvesting data), while e-commerce and online services were growing quickly. By the time Chrome’s password manager came around, I had already signed up for dozens of sites using the same password.
I eventually set up a few safeguards as well, including signing up for Have I Been Pwned updates and keeping an eye on Google Password Manager’s notifications for leaked passwords. I did eventually stop using the password because password managers allowed me to generate much more complex credentials without needing to remember them. I could also easily store and access passwords from my phone or my browser, meaning that these secure credentials applied to new app sign-ups as well.
Over the years, I also started changing some of my most important accounts, as well as the ones I was most concerned about when it came to leaks. My Facebook password has long-since changed, along with my primary Google account. At the same time, though, I didn’t realize how much of a trail of reused passwords I had left behind. These were mostly sites I no longer used, so they fell to the back of my mind.
Despite switching to different passwords and a password manager, I didn't realize the trail of reused passwords I had left behind.
I only realized just how much I had reused the same password when it was already compromised. I visited my Pass Monitor feature in Proton Pass and discovered I had used the same password over 140 times. A few of these were false positives, since they were the same account with slightly different URLs saved. A few had also already been updated. Luckily, these weren’t identical credentials — the password was spread out across different usernames and email addresses.
But the conclusion was clear: I had spent years in the early 2010s signing up for a large number of online accounts with the same password. Also, despite changing some of my most-used accounts, I had missed some in my cleanup. This included my secondary Gmail account and my Reddit account.
A single breach exposed countless accounts
About a month ago, I received an email from a service I no longer use, stating that my data may have been compromised. It was frustrating because the app I signed up for had been rebranded and integrated into another app, so I had no idea what account information was stored in it besides my email address. The disclosure noted that encrypted passwords were included, but didn’t clarify what that meant. Ever the optimist, I hoped this meant the actual passwords were still protected by encryption.
Google flagged 11 vulnerable accounts, but Proton Pass allowed me to see the true extent of the breach's consequences.
However, last week, Google sent a critical security alert noting that my password had appeared online. It flagged 11 accounts that were affected, including the defunct app that had been breached. I finally found out which password I had used for the app, and my stomach sank when I realized it was the holy grail password of my student days.
Knowing that I had relied on this password for years, I also knew that the count of 11 compromised logins was too low. Google Password Manager didn’t let me search for accounts that shared the same password, so I moved to Proton Pass. And that’s when I saw the throat-lump-inducing total of 140 logins sharing the same password.
How I finally fixed it
Oh no, the consequences of my actions. When I saw how many times I had reused the password, I wanted to kick myself. However, rather than lingering on a past I couldn’t change, I decided to fix what I could. This meant going scorched earth on the password.
As mentioned, the password was spread across multiple usernames and email addresses. However, I didn’t want to risk someone linking my leaked email address and password with other accounts and breaching those. As a result, I decided to change every single login that included the password.
First, I started off with Google’s Password Manager dashboard. The tool allowed me to follow links to the sites with breached passwords. Not every password reset link worked, but it did prove quicker than manually visiting every site myself. The problem was that Google had only flagged 11 accounts with the leaked password. I reset the passwords for the remaining sites, then moved to Proton Pass.
When I saw how many times I had reused the password, I wanted to kick myself.
With Proton Pass, I could use the Pass Monitor dashboard to find which logins used the same password. This proved helpful because it flagged the same password across different accounts, not only my primary Google account.
I prioritized the most vulnerable services first — those that exactly matched my leaked credentials. I then moved on to any service that included the leaked email address but a different username. Finally, I reset the services with different email addresses and the same password.
The main hurdle was services that no longer existed or that no longer worked correctly. I couldn’t delete these accounts or even reset their passwords. However, at least every account that matched their credentials had been changed.
My Proton Pass browser extension made it easy to generate new passwords and update the credentials. This saved a lot of time while going through all the logins. I also used its mobile app when resetting passwords using apps on my phone.
I prioritized the most vulnerable services, then whittled down the list of other reused passwords by resetting account credentials.
Eventually, I managed to change all the remaining accounts. I kept the logins for defunct sites in Proton Pass, since if those ever get breached, I want to be able to easily check which credentials were used. The entire process took two afternoons.
My next-most-reused password was used 34 times, though some of the credentials were duplicates for the same account. However, I went ahead and changed these too. I also decided to change the passwords for both of my Google accounts to something both secure and memorable, out of an abundance of caution.
After my war on reused passwords, I feel a lot better about my online security. I still have to watch out for scams, since over the years, my phone number and email have been leaked in breaches. It’s frustrating that many of the places we trust with our data fail to secure it. However, I at least know that my own passwords won’t be the weak point in my online security anymore.
results.summary:
A security breach revealed that a user had reused a single password across 140 different online accounts, prompting a comprehensive effort to secure their digital identity.

### Key Points
- The user discovered 140 accounts shared a single password after a data breach notification triggered a security audit using Proton Pass.
- Google Password Manager initially flagged only 11 vulnerable accounts, failing to identify the full extent of the credential reuse.
- The remediation process involved prioritizing high-risk services and using password manager tools to generate and update unique credentials for every affected site.
- The user successfully mitigated the risk by systematically resetting passwords over two afternoons, including secondary accounts like Gmail and Reddit.
- Defunct services that could not be accessed for password resets were retained in the password manager to track potential future exposure.

### Why it Matters
Password reuse creates a "domino effect" where a single data breach at one minor service can compromise numerous other, more sensitive accounts. This incident highlights the necessity of using dedicated password managers to audit credential security and ensure that every online account utilizes a unique, complex password.

results.title: Over half of PC gamers are still on 1080p in 2026, and the reason isn't the monitors
results.author: Abhinav Raj
results.content:
The Steam Hardware Survey is perhaps one of the most illustrative data sets that indicates the reality of where the consumer market is at. In my many years of going through the survey, a lot has changed, except one category that seems to move slower than the others. In the latest available June 2026 survey, 51.12% of players are reportedly still running 1080p as their primary display. If you were to compare this from three years ago, it was about 61.17% in September 2023, so it is falling, but slowly enough that half the platform is still sitting there.
At a cursory glance, it would seem as though that monitor pricing is holding gamers back, and that people are usually last to upgrade their display. That's something that I assumed, at least until I checked the pricing trends for 1440p monitors. The numbers were low enough to disregard this theory, and so the blame moved onto a component that most people aren't thinking of when going through the survey.
The monitors haven't been the most expensive part of the transition for a while
You can find half a dozen 1440p panels under $200 without trying
A fortnight ago, PC Gamer published a list of six highly capable and feature-packed 1440p gaming monitors under $200, with the entry price being as low as $110. A 27-inch 1440p IPS monitor running at 180Hz would set one back about $130. If you wanted an entry-level OLED screen, Alienware recently released a 1440p 240Hz panel at $349, which means the transition to the highly sought-after panel is no longer a thousand-dollar affair.
Evidently, displays are one of the few PC components that have gotten cheaper this year while everything else has gotten more expensive. Market research analysts at Omdia provide a reason for this, stating that this price democratization is being driven by Korean panel manufacturers reallocating their production lines to focus on monitor displays over TV panels. According to the firm's July 2026 report, OLED monitor display shipments are set to surge by 34% as manufacturers pivot Gen 8.5 fabrication plant capacity to desktop panels, which is sparking a wave of supply-side price cuts.
So clearly, half the PC platform isn't sitting at 1080p because a better monitor is unaffordable. With display prices plummeting, the barrier to high-resolution gaming seems to have shifted from the monitor to the machine itself. The obvious culprit, of course, seems to be GPU pricing.
The actual cost of 1440p gaming is the VRAM
And the entry price shows no signs of dropping
It has been established that buying the screen is the easy part. However, keeping the games running at 1440p and keeping them running well enough to justify the price of a better panel and refresh rate is where things have gotten a lot more expensive. And a lot of the latter has got to do with how much VRAM the user's GPU has.
Most hardware manufacturers such as NZXT, tech forums and credible tech YouTubers recommend at least 12GB of VRAM to deliver a smooth 1440p gaming experience on high or ultra settings, and the problem seems to be the fact that most setups simply don't have it, and are most often priced out of it. After all, the very same Steam Hardware Survey from June 2026 states that the most popular VRAM configuration is 8GB, across a quarter of the player base.
What exacerbates the problem further is that GPUs with higher VRAM configurations have been steadily sliding out of reach for many consumers month after month, given the pricing pressure owed primarily (if not only) to the DRAM crisis.
Nvidia has raised GPU kit prices for board partners repeatedly over the last few months, following a 10-15% increase in January 2026 and a narrower one in May. The latest markup from Team Green only came a few days ago, when it notified distributors of the third hike this year alone, raising prices by 20–30% across the entire RTX stack. AMD has followed suit and lifted its GPU-GDDR prices and notified AIB partners of a 10% or higher price increase on those kits effective this month. Naturally, 1440p cards are amongst some of the worst hit.
| GPU Model | Architecture | VRAM | Average US Street Price (July 2026) | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Radeon RX 7700 XT | RDNA 3 | 12GB GDDR6 | $409 | 
| GeForce RTX 4070 | Ada Lovelace | 12GB GDDR6X | $570 | 
| GeForce RTX 5070 | Blackwell | 12GB GDDR7 | $614 | 
| GeForce RTX 4070 Super | Ada Lovelace | 12GB GDDR6X | $674 | 
| GeForce RTX 4070 Ti | Ada Lovelace | 12GB GDDR6X | $693 | 
The card I bought three times is the one that stopped making sense
Mid-range meant value, and the VRAM economics completely broke it
I've been gaming at 1440p since 2021, and every single card I have bought to do it came from the same pricing tier. Upper mid-range, GeForce, with, of course, the closest Radeon competitor coming into the consideration every time. That segment is precisely where I believed the best price-to-performance lived, and it was tailor-made for my output resolution. 1440p has always been the sensible place for me to game for years, and most analysts over the past decade have also argued that it's where the "sweet spot" between performance and visual fidelity exists, at the right price for the right card.
Perhaps one of the most defining aspects of GPUs in this range is the generous 12–16GB VRAM allocation, but in these troubled times when the latest GDDR7 memory accounts for the bulk of the bill of materials, the price-to-performance math doesn't skew in the favor of the consumer buying in this segment. Suffice it to say, the VRAM allocation itself seems to have become the Achilles' Heel of the mid-range.
The VRAM math priced out the other half from 1440p gaming
Perhaps the most regrettable aspect of it all is what the DRAM crisis has done to the upgrade path of the budget gamer. For anyone who wishes to leave 1080p behind, a mid-range card with 12GB of VRAM was always the next logical step. The pricing, and as prohibitive as it has become, has turned that straightforward progression into a financial decision that many would just not sign off on.
results.summary:
The June 2026 Steam Hardware Survey reveals that 51.12% of users remain on 1080p displays, as rising GPU costs and VRAM requirements hinder the transition to 1440p gaming.

### Key Points
- Over half of Steam users still utilize 1080p monitors, despite 1440p panels becoming increasingly affordable with entry-level options available for under $200.
- Omdia reports that OLED monitor shipments are projected to rise by 34% as manufacturers shift production capacity toward desktop panels.
- Most experts recommend at least 12GB of VRAM for smooth 1440p performance, yet 25% of the Steam user base currently relies on 8GB configurations.
- Nvidia and AMD have implemented multiple price hikes in 2026, with Nvidia raising costs across its RTX stack by 20–30% due to the ongoing DRAM crisis.
- Mid-range graphics cards, once considered the "sweet spot" for 1440p gaming, have seen significant price increases, making them less accessible for budget-conscious consumers.

### Why it Matters
The shift toward higher-resolution gaming is currently stalled not by monitor costs, but by the rising price of the graphics hardware required to power them. This trend forces consumers to choose between staying at 1080p or paying a premium for the VRAM necessary to support modern 1440p gaming standards.

results.title: Trump’s Truth Social API Is a Blatantly Corrupt Favor to Wall Street
results.author: Dylan Gyauch-Lewis
results.content:
Dylan is a senior researcher at the Revolving Door Project, where she leads RDP’s Economic Media Project.
For the low, low price of $100,000 a month, the ever-oxymoronic Truth Social is now selling direct access to its most important posts — or, in the firm’s preferred parlance, “truths” — to Wall Street. That’s an expedited lane to access statements and data from the president of the United States and other government officials, which have significant potential to move financial markets, ahead of us suckers in the general public.
This sort of product, called an Application Processing Interface, or API, is not a particularly unusual offering for a social media company in the abstract. But Truth API, which launched today, is uniquely positioned to fuel blatant presidential graft.
The move has been rightly called “brazen corruption,” “the president’s most desperate grift yet,” and a “clear and unacceptable pathway for corruption.” In a letter to the Securities and Exchange Commission, Sens. Adam Schiff and Elizabeth Warren called the offering “an outrageous abuse of the President’s office for his personal benefit that undermines everyday investors and the integrity of our markets, while enriching Wall Street and other wealthy insiders.” All of that is true, but Truth API doesn’t stop at creating a new pathway to funnel de facto bribes to Trump; it also seeks to functionally merge the provision of a public good with a for-profit company.
It has become de facto administration policy for high-ranking government officials to make official announcements on Truth Social without going through traditional press offices. Trump has also set a new standard for blurring the lines between his communications as a public official and a private citizen.
For nearly half a century, communications from the president have been recognized as the property of the United States, not the president himself. Under the Presidential Records Act, any documents (with some carve-outs for national security and personal records like journals and diaries) that are “created or received by the President … in the course of conducting activities which relate to or have an effect upon the carrying out of the constitutional, statutory, or other official or ceremonial duties of the President” are subject to the United States’ “complete ownership, possession, and control.”
In other words, selling expedited access to such statements is effectively privatizing a public asset. That might be part of the reason why, this spring, Trump’s Department of Justice Office of Legal Counsel issued an opinion that argues the heretofore uncontroversial Presidential Records Act is unconstitutional.
Trump owns a 41 percent stake in Truth Social’s parent company, Trump Media & Technology Group. In December 2024, all of his shares were transferred into Trump’s revocable trust, which is overseen by Donald Trump Jr. At the time, it was a 52 percent stake, worth about $4 billion against the company’s total valuation of $7.5 billion. Those TMTG shares (which are of course traded under the narcissistic ticker DJT) represent a major part of the president’s total wealth. While his stake in the company is now valued at (only!) $1.2 billion, it still represents 18 percent of Trump’s overall wealth, which Forbes estimated to be $6.5 billion.
And while Truth Social has become a pillar of the Trump business empire, it is also a pillar of sand. Truth Social hemorrhages money: In 2024, it only brought in $3.6 million and had a net loss of more than $400 million. Last year was even worse: Revenue ticked up slightly to $3.68 million, but its net loss soared to more than $700 million. The company’s value is now less than one-fourth of what it was in its spring 2024 heyday. That’s a lot of money on board a sinking ship.
TMTG tried to find income streams from branching out into prediction markets, cryptocurrency issuing, bitcoin investment, and nuclear energy production (perhaps a nod to Trump’s physicist Uncle John). But none of these maneuvers have stopped the bleeding.
This latest plan to sell the API might finally be the path to profitability that TMTG so desperately needs. At its core, what an API does is provide a data feed directly into a particular software program, in this case financial trading terminals. So even though the company insisted to the Wall Street Journal that “Truth API is designed to deliver posts the instant they are made public to everyone, not before,” it still represents priority access to government officials’ statements because anyone not paying for the service will be unable to process the information at the same pace as subscribers, letting professional traders and hedge funds outpace the market and reap the benefits.
In modern financial markets, an advantage of even fractions of a second can be decisive — and can provide the opportunity to reap huge profits. This is the sitting president directly selling financial powerhouses a significant edge from the very heart of the federal government for a cool $100,000 a month (or a paltry $60,000 if you opt for a multi-year subscription!).
This entire sordid arrangement already reeks of corruption, but the stench grows stronger when juxtaposed with this administration’s propensity to mistakenly, illegally, and/or prematurely release information when they aren’t supposed to, and not infrequently on Truth Social. Trump’s presidency has always been defined by the degradation of our sense of shared reality and by rampant corruption. There’s no better metaphor than sticking a price tag on the “truths” coming out of the administration.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.

results.summary:
Trump Media & Technology Group has launched a $100,000-per-month API service providing Wall Street firms with expedited, automated access to official government statements posted on the Truth Social platform.

### Key Points
- The Truth API allows financial institutions to ingest presidential communications into trading terminals faster than the general public can access them.
- Donald Trump maintains an 18% stake in Trump Media & Technology Group, which reported a net loss exceeding $700 million in the previous year.
- Sens. Adam Schiff and Elizabeth Warren have formally requested an SEC investigation, citing concerns over market integrity and potential presidential corruption.
- The service bypasses traditional press office channels, effectively monetizing official government communications as a private corporate product.

### Why it Matters
This arrangement raises significant ethical and legal questions regarding the privatization of public records and the potential for insider trading based on government announcements. By selling a speed advantage to wealthy investors, the administration risks undermining fair market access and blurring the lines between official duties and personal financial gain.

results.title: ‘Plug-in batteries are the real game-changer’: I talked to Octopus Energy and Anker about the home energy revolution than could soon be 'bigger than solar' for millions
results.author: mark.wilson@futurenet.com (Mark Wilson) , Mark Wilson
results.content:
It's typical, you wait for ages for a home energy revolution and then two come along at once — or at least that's what appears to be happening in the UK.
You've probably heard about the first landmark moment. 'Plug-in solar' hit the headlines last week when the UK government announced that small, solar panel kits that feed electricity directly into your standard home socket can legally go on sale from August 27.
That's a big deal. Plug-in solar means that millions of people who have traditionally been locked out of generating their own clean electricity — renters and flat owners, for example — will be able to join the residential solar party, albeit on a more modest scale.
But not everyone was celebrating wildly with biodegradable confetti. Across the country, energy nerds bemoaned one glaring omission in the government's new legislation — a legal pathway for 'plug-in batteries'.
For many, these small home batteries — think a mini Tesla Powerwall that plugs into a standard wall socket — are the "real game-changer", as Octopus Energy and Anker both described them to me. That's because they promise to be even more accessible than plug-in solar and act as a money-saving brain that makes your home an active part of a smarter UK electricity grid.
Bold claims indeed, so I spoke to four of the biggest players in this burgeoning space — Anker, Octopus Energy, EcoFlow and Windfall Energy — along with the UK government to find out when plug-in batteries might be coming, what the drawbacks are and, most importantly, how much you can really expect to save...
When are they coming?
The main premise of plug-in home batteries, like the Windfall Battery above, is simple — they charge automatically using cheap-rate electricity (usually at night), then discharge that electricity around your home during more expensive peak-rate periods. "Even without solar panels, a plug-in battery delivers meaningful savings through grid arbitrage alone," Anker Solix's EU CEO, Kelvin Cao, tells me. Savings estimates range from between £100-£400 per year, depending on your battery, tariff and usage.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Great, so when exactly will they become legal in the UK? When I asked the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ), the official answer was predictably vague. "We are rolling out plug-in solar, which will be quickest to reach the market — helping to bring bills down for good," a DESNZ spokesperson said.
Plug-in batteries are smart energy storage devices that connect to your home's electrical network through a standard wall socket, without any professional installation. They automatically charge from the grid when electricity is cheap and release energy back into your home during peak-rate hours to cut your energy bills. They can work on their own or alongside solar. While they're not currently legal in the UK, that could potentially change soon.
The DESNZ told me its main focus right now is plug-in solar kits and that plug-in batteries have their own technical and regulatory hurdles, which it's currently investigating. Still, there are hopes that grid-connected batteries that plug into your wall socket could be legalised within the next year.
Several big players are quietly preparing plug-in batteries — which are already available in countries like Germany — for a UK launch. Anker, for example, has built a page for its Solix Solarbank 4 that clearly explains the benefits of plug-in batteries, should they become legalised in the UK. "We are eager to support the rise of the plug-in era in the UK and become part of its evolving energy landscape," Anker Solix's EU CEO, Kelvin Cao, told me.
Octopus Energy also recently announced that its new plug-in Nook Cube battery will go on sale sometime in 2027. More confident on the timescale is Windfall Energy, a London startup that's designed the best-looking piece of home energy kit I've seen for a while, the Windfall Battery.
"I was at a roundtable with a Minister of Parliament about a month ago, and everyone there was pretty much calling for batteries to come hot on the heels of plug-in solar," Windfall Energy's co-founder Rob Hallifax told me.
So when is Windfall expecting to start selling its 2.5 kWh home battery, which has an RRP of £1,200 and had previously been slated to ship in autumn? "Winter is more likely now. We want to time it with the plug-in regulations. It’s looking like the end of this year, early next," he added.
Why now?
You'll probably have noticed that the UK has been on an energy rollercoaster that can technically be described as 'not fun'.
Back in the late 1990s and early 2000s, inflation-adjusted gas and electricity prices were actually stable or even falling. But there was a huge spike for both in early 2022 and they've never returned to pre-energy crisis levels. Electricity prices are still 13% higher than in January 2020, according to the UK government, and they continue to move in the wrong direction.
Plug-in batteries promise to be, if not a cure, then at least a much-needed pain killer for our energy bills headache. They're emerging now because of three things — falling prices for lithium-iron-phosphate (LFP) batteries, the easing of electrical regulations in some regions (Germany created the world's first dedicated plug-in solar product standard in late 2025), and soaring wholesale gas prices that are reflected in the graph above.
As Anker's Kelvin Cao tells me, this has "reshaped how European households think about electricity". Unfortunately, that double-digit increase in energy prices is also "unlikely to come down any time soon". That's why Germany started the trend, and the UK is (hopefully) about to follow.
So how exactly do plug-in batteries save you money? "There’s two parts to the price saving," Windfall Energy's co-founder Rob Hallifax tells me. "The simple one is just the price arbitrage. So if you're paying 10p at night and 30p in the day for electricity per kilowatt hour, then you buy it at 10p, use it when it's 30p, you're saving 20p per kilowatt hour," he says.
That part's pretty simple — with the Windfall Battery, this 'buy low, use when prices skyrocket' approach makes up about £168 of its promised £250 per year savings. But there are also extra savings from getting your plug-in battery really singing in tune with the electricity network.
The UK grid acts a bit like a giant smart thermostat, signaling when the system needs more or less electricity, and the idea is that energy suppliers could follow by telling plug-in home batteries when to charge and discharge. Smaller plug-in batteries would likely be capped at an 800W output (without professional installation), so wouldn't be exporting power to the grid. But they could still play a role in balancing demand.
This makes tariffs the second big factor in the money-saving potential of plug-in batteries — and that's something Octopus Energy has been a UK leader in.
"The energy sector overall has not really embraced the fact that you can just offer different types of products to different types of consumer customer groups," Alex Schoch, Group Director for Flexibility at Octopus Energy, tells me. "Of our eight million customers, 1.2 million are on some kind of smart tariff," he adds.
Octopus Energy told me there could potentially be dedicated plug-in battery tariffs or bolt-ons for existing ones. If you've ever been baffled by choosing the right energy tariff, this could also get simpler thanks to plug-in batteries.
"I equate it to the evolution of mobile phone plans," Octopus Energy's Alex Schoch tells me. "First, they were incredibly generic. Then they got so complicated that Carphone Warehouse came into being just to explain the complexity. And now we’re at a stage where we create hyper-personalised plans based on your needs as a consumer. We’re on that same journey when it comes to energy".
But doesn't this also demand a lot of trust in energy companies? Windfall Energy's Rob Hallifax agrees, but thinks falling bills will ultimately convince consumers. "It's their (consumers'] battery, they're in control of it, but the energy company is controlling it a bit to help them maximize the savings," he says. "The consumer has to trust that the energy company is doing this to save them money, and I think that will come when they see their bills go down," he adds.
What's the catch?
Clearly, plug-in batteries won't be a magic wand for everyone's bills, even if the batteries could be subsidised or even given away for free by the UK government to lower-income households, as the i Paper reported recently (the DESNZ declined to comment on this when I asked).
For most plug-in batteries, the payback period (the time it takes for savings to cover the cost of the battery) is expected to be around 3-4 for years, so not exactly a financial quick fix. The Windfall Battery promises annual savings of £250 (with an RRP of £1,200), while Anker tells me that the larger Solix Solarbank 4 on a dynamic tariff like Octopus Agile could save you just under £400 per year. That battery has no UK price yet, but retails for €1,999 in Europe (around £1,700).
The other concern raised by skeptics is safety. Is allowing potentially millions of households to connect batteries to their electricity networks without professional installation really a good idea? Windfall Energy's Rob Hallifax acknowledges that it's an understandable concern. "People see a battery, and they think of scooters and fires, and there some valid concerns. Obviously, safety is critically important, and just one battery fire would be one too many," he says.
"But modern batteries are generally extremely safe,' he adds. "There are some studies out of Germany now where they compare batteries to EVs and other home appliances. One headline is that they’re typically about as safe as a washing machine," he adds. The other common comparison is with fan heaters, which are legal in the UK but carry a higher risk of 'user error' incidents than plug-in batteries.
Still, the added complexities of grid-charging batteries mean some agree with the UK government's top-dipping approach. EcoFlow, one of the biggest global players in home batteries, is among them. "We're aware and completely understand that these things take time," Lorna Wallace-Smith (EcoFlow's Head of UK PR) told me. "The fact that they were able to move forward with at least one step is is great" she added.
But hasn't Germany's rapid adoption of both plug-in solar and home batteries shown it's safe? "I think that's something we should learn from, as well as not fast-track into something without knowing it's absolutely built for UK homes," she added.
Could they outshine solar?
Despite these concerns, it seems clear that plug-in batteries have the potential to eclipse the more complex plug-in solar kits in the UK — and most of the experts I spoke to agreed.
"They are the fundamental great equalizer," says Octopus' Alex Schoch on plug-in batteries. "It’s such an important thing for renters because you can then take it with you to your next place," he adds.
"I think in the next couple of years we will see plug-in batteries really be the transformational scale deployment. I think it has the potential of being a mass market thing even faster than solar," he predicts.
Windfall Energy's Rob Hallifax naturally agrees when comparing plug-in batteries to their solar equivalent. "There are 28 million homes in the UK and about half of them are either rented or flats and small homes. So more people could get them, millions, and there’s also the benefit to the grid and to the system," he says.
There is one other obvious comparison with an accessory that's cheap, easy to use and promises to save you money. "We use air fryers as quite a good example. Four or five years ago they just came from nowhere and suddenly half the country has one," he says.
But wouldn't an 'air fryer' level of popularity also cause a problem for plug-in batteries? After all, a lot of their money-saving potential comes from tapping into today's so-called 'delta' between cheap-rate and peak-rate electricity. If plug-in batteries help to solve the imbalance of today's grid demand — and tariffs are adjusted to reflect that — could that start to diminish their savings potential?
"I think yes and no," says Windfall Energy's Rob Hallifax. "So maybe in 50 years the whole grid will be sort of perfect. I think the fundamental thing is that if you have renewable generation, that's always going to be variable. That's just the nature of the world. And so somewhere in the system, storage has to be part of it," he adds.
Octopus Energy's Alex Schoch agrees that such a change would be a long way off. "In theory, yes." he says in response to my pessimistic scenario. "But I would actually say the length of time here is measured in decades, not in a sub-decade quantum," he adds.
However, he does note that a similar process is already happening. "We've had such an explosion of solar in the UK over the last few years that now during Spring and Summer, a lot of the cheapest wholesale price electricity times are actually late morning, early afternoon, mid afternoon, and no longer overnight," he notes.
Charging ahead
The legalisation of plug-in batteries in the UK appears to be a matter of 'when' not 'if'. As a flat owner in south west London with no roof and only a limited appetite for plug-in solar, I'm right in the target market — and will certainly be interested when that moment comes.
But it also won't be an impulse buy where I snap up the first thing I see Amazon. "The biggest pitfall to avoid is making decision on price alone," says Anker's Kelvin Cao. "Now that plug-in solar has regulatory approval, the UK market will attract a wave of low-cost imports, some of which will be excellent and some of which will not. This will be a similar problem once the plug-in batteries are legalised," he warns.
"A battery that cuts corners on cell quality, protective engineering and compliance with applicable safety standards might look more attractive on its price tag, but it will not deliver the same reliability over the 10 to 15 years that a household should reasonably expect," he adds. In other words, buying cheap could backfire when it comes to savings.
So what exactly should you look for when plug-in batteries are legalised? "As a baseline, consumers should look for durable LFP battery cells, a high cycle life, robust protection against weather and corrosion, and integrated safeguards against electrical and thermal risks," Kelvin Cao says.
"They'll probably also say that the product must be listed on the Energy Networks Association (ENA) Type Test Register to demonstrate that its protection settings meet G98 requirements," adds Windfall Energy's Rob Hallifax.
A real-world view
A large number of early adopters are already getting a taste of the benefits of a battery-only setup. One of those is TechRadar contributor Mark Pickavance, who wrote our EcoFlow Stream Ultra X review (which is well worth a read).
I caught up with him to see how it's going and he continues to be impressed. He told me that his monthly energy costs are down by about £40 a month with his setup (which was installed with the help of an electrician), and you could get most of that from a single Ultra X.
The only problem is that this stuff can get addictive. "I started with the premise of using just a battery, but once you have one the logical progression is solar. However, for people renting, it's the ideal solution, and if you use an Economy 7-like tariff (Octopus Go), you can take a chunk out of your costs," he said.
The arrival of plug-in solar from August could, then, be a good dry run of what to expect when plug-in batteries arrive. The big differences between residential buildings between Germany and the UK could mean plug-in solar doesn't quite take off in the same way in the UK, but Anker's Kelvin Cao remains bullish.
"This is no longer a niche movement. Germany passed one million officially registered plug-in solar systems in 2025, with around 430,000 new systems registered during that year alone," he notes. If plug-in batteries follow a similar pattern in the UK, that could have big consequences for energy bills — and the UK's grid as a whole.

Mark is TechRadar's Senior news editor. Having worked in tech journalism for a ludicrous 17 years, Mark is now attempting to break the world record for the number of camera bags hoarded by one person. He was previously Cameras Editor at both TechRadar and Trusted Reviews, Acting editor on Stuff.tv, as well as Features editor and Reviews editor on Stuff magazine. As a freelancer, he's contributed to titles including The Sunday Times, FourFourTwo and Arena. And in a former life, he also won The Daily Telegraph's Young Sportswriter of the Year. results.title: SEC to review Nasdaq bitcoin options approval after CME challenge
results.author: Francisco Rodrigues
results.content:
SEC to review Nasdaq bitcoin options approval after CME challenge
CME argues that because bitcoin is a commodity, options tied to its value fall under CFTC jurisdiction, not the SEC's authority.
- The SEC has frozen Nasdaq's approval of QBTC bitcoin options to reconsider the decision following a legal challenge from CME Group.
- CME argues that because bitcoin is a commodity, options tied to its value fall under the CFTC’s jurisdiction, not the SEC’s.
- The approval remains suspended while the SEC reviews the dispute, with interested parties invited to submit comments by Aug. 24.
The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has paused Nasdaq's approval of cash-settled bitcoin index options and will reconsider the decision following a legal challenge from CME Group, the agency said in an order released for public inspection on July 31.
Back in May, the SEC granted Nasdaq PHLX conditional approval to list cash-settled bitcoin index options under the ticker QBTC. The product still required exemptions from the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) before it could launch.
CME Group challenged the approval in June, arguing that bitcoin is a commodity and, as such, options tied directly to its value fall under the CFTC’s exclusive jurisdiction rather than the SEC’s.
If the CME is right, the SEC would have no authority to approve QBTC, and Nasdaq would need to register as a CFTC-regulated futures or swaps venue, or redesign the contracts to track a security such as a spot bitcoin exchange-traded fund.
The CME already operates regulated bitcoin futures and options markets, while Nasdaq’s QBTC would compete for the same trading activity without Nasdaq registering under the CFTC framework that governs the CME.
The petition also warned that the approval could set a precedent allowing securities exchanges to list derivatives on other commodities. Nasdaq’s proposed contracts would use CME CF benchmarks for both their underlying index and final settlement price.
The order keeps the approval frozen and gives interested parties until Aug. 24 to submit statements supporting or opposing it. The stay has been in place since CME filed notice of its challenge on June 11.
The SEC’s May approval envisioned the CFTC granting exemptions, which would allow Nasdaq and the Options Clearing Corporation to offer the product through the securities market. The CME argued that the agencies cannot use exemptions to transfer a product from one regulator to another.
QBTC will remain suspended while the full commission reviews the earlier approval.
Binance remains crypto’s leading exchange, expanding from spot and derivatives into RWAs, payments, savings, yield, and broader financial services.
Why it matters:
Binance remains crypto’s leading exchange, expanding from spot and derivatives into RWAs, payments, savings, yield, and broader financial services.

results.title: AI can help pinpoint a top CEO candidate. The harder part is persuading them to take the job.
results.author: Sarah E. Needleman
results.content:
AI is accelerating many parts of executive-level hiring, though other parts remain constrained by distinctly human obstacles.
Recruiters say homing in on suitable candidates can account for as much as half the work in high-stakes C-suite job searches. AI can speed up that process by mapping the market, surfacing names, combing through years of internal notes, and suggesting unconventional talent pools.
"The identification of candidates is going to become commoditized," said Marty Parker, CEO of Waterstone Human Capital, an executive search and culture advisory firm.
Meanwhile, other parts of the recruiting process remain slow because they still depend heavily on people, from coordinating and conducting interviews with busy candidates to exercising judgment, building consensus, and persuading an executive to make a move.
"All of those things are irreducibly human," said Umesh Ramakrishnan, chief strategy officer of executive search firm Kingsley Gate. Now, he added, AI "takes care of everything else."
What AI can do
Waterstone saw AI's potential at the start of an ongoing search for an executive to oversee a jewelry company's high-tech manufacturing operation. The firm had initially focused on recruiting from other jewelry businesses when the company's proprietary AI tool suggested looking to the dental tech industry, where similar precision machinery is used to make veneers, crowns, and other tiny, intricate products.
"Who would consider dental manufacturing with jewelers?" Parker said. "You just wouldn't. It's not obvious."
Search firms are also using AI to mine years of interview notes to identify prospective candidates.
Matthew Siegel, a principal at Korn Ferry, said a consultant might recall being impressed by someone at a particular company but forget the person's name or what stood out. AI can retrieve the likely match and the earlier observations behind that impression, he said.
"It's just a terrific example of AI as a force multiplier, just making us more effective," Siegel said.
Beyond candidate research, AI is helping to automate the administrative work surrounding a search.
Nathan Clauss, CEO and managing partner of tech-focused search firm Talent SDK, said recruiters are increasingly building their own AI tools that integrate with internal messaging and applicant-tracking systems, organize information across platforms, and eliminate manual steps. For example, AI can read candidate emails and note why someone is or isn't interested in a role.
By reducing those repetitive tasks, Clauss said AI has allowed his sourcing team to accomplish two to three times as much in a day as they might have several years ago.
"I haven't fired any of my sourcers," he said. "They've just gotten way more productive."
AI is informing later stages of a search, too. Waterstone's AI tool was trained on 23 years of data about organizational culture and executive hiring. Parker said it can suggest interview questions, presentations, and exercises designed to reveal how finalists think and behave. The technology doesn't, however, evaluate candidates' performance.
"It gives us the experience," Parker said of the model. "We then apply our judgment."
What still takes people
For all the time AI can save on research and administrative work, recruiters said it hasn't altered the parts of executive search that require interpretation, trust, and persuasion.
Case in point: As more executives claim AI expertise, recruiters still have to determine for themselves whose experience is genuine. Jeff Markham, a partner at executive search firm Parker Remick, said that may involve contacting a candidate's references and other industry sources to verify that the individual still "gets their hands on the keyboard."
Ramakrishnan said assessing a C-suite candidate can require observing the person outside a formal interview. A recruiter may notice nonverbal behavior that would never surface in a résumé or prepared response.
"Only a human being can sit with the CEO candidate at dinner and watch for the nonverbal things that he or she does," Ramakrishnan said.
AI hasn't transformed the courtship, either. Winning over a candidate still requires understanding the company, the opportunity, and what might motivate them to leave their current post, said Mike Doud, executive vice president, North America, at The Barton Partnership, an executive search firm.
Recruiters need to study candidates' careers as well as the cultures, bureaucracies, and internal politics of the companies where they have worked, he said. Recruiters also need a similarly nuanced understanding of the client to determine whether the client and the candidates they are recommending for top jobs are a match.
Recruiters still have to "sell the opportunity," Doud said, because an executive move is "a life-changing event," not simply another job.
results.summary:
Executive search firms are increasingly integrating artificial intelligence to accelerate candidate identification and administrative tasks, while reserving complex judgment and relationship-building for human recruiters in high-stakes hiring.

### Key Points
- AI tools now map markets and suggest unconventional talent pools, such as identifying dental tech experts for jewelry manufacturing roles.
- Search firms like Korn Ferry use AI to mine years of internal interview notes and retrieve specific candidate observations.
- Automation of administrative tasks, such as organizing emails and tracking systems, has reportedly doubled or tripled daily productivity for sourcing teams.
- Proprietary models trained on decades of hiring data assist recruiters by generating interview questions and behavioral exercises for executive finalists.
- Human recruiters remain essential for verifying technical expertise, interpreting nonverbal cues, and persuading executives to accept life-changing career moves.

### Why it Matters
The integration of AI into executive search shifts the recruiter's role from manual data gathering to high-level strategic advising and relationship management. While technology significantly increases efficiency in the early stages of hiring, the reliance on human judgment for final placements ensures that trust and cultural fit remain central to corporate leadership transitions.

results.title: CISA Alert: Water Sector PLC Targeting
results.author: Alex Gartner
results.content:
Introduction
CISA issued an alert on July 30, 2026 warning that threat actors are increasingly targeting internet-exposed programmable logic controllers (PLCs) in the Water and Wastewater Systems (WWS) sector, in some cases modifying passwords to lock out operators and disconnecting devices by changing their IP addresses, resulting in boil-water notices and sustained manual operations. CISA named Rockwell Automation/Allen-Bradley, Siemens, and Schneider Electric equipment and flagged cellular modems as a common blind spot in routine attack-surface scans. This report characterizes current Censys-observed internet exposure for each named vendor: 4,148 Rockwell/Allen-Bradley EtherNet/IP hosts, 4,117 Siemens SIMATIC S7-1200 hosts, and 2,072 Schneider Electric hosts (vendor-wide, not PLC-scoped), all as of the 2026-07-30 snapshot. This is an exposure characterization only: it does not confirm that any specific host is a victim of the activity CISA describes.
Advisory Context
The following paraphrases the CISA alert as supplied by the user for this report; it was not independently re-fetched from cisa.gov in this session.
CISA is observing a significant increase in threat actors targeting programmable logic controllers (PLCs) in the Water and Wastewater Systems (WWS) Sector. CISA urges critical infrastructure owners, operators, and integrators to remove publicly exposed PLCs and other operational technology (OT) from the internet as soon as possible. Observed actor behavior includes modifying PLC passwords to lock out operators and disconnecting PLCs by changing their IP addresses, producing boil-water notices and sustained manual operations at affected utilities.
Targeting affects water entities of all sizes, including organizations with mature cybersecurity processes. CISA specifically flags cellular modems installed by operators, vendors, or system integrators as a common blind spot: these connections may be undocumented and excluded from routine attack-surface scans. Owners of Rockwell Automation MicroLogix 1400 controllers are directed to Rockwell’s guidance for restoring access when a controller password is unknown.
CISA-Recommended Mitigations
- Disconnect the PLC from the internet; route remote access through a VPN or gateway device, not directly to the PLC.
- Enable password protection and change default passwords.
- Allowlist IPs to permit remote access only from known engineering laptops or other critical OT assets.
This report addresses the exposure-characterization question only — current internet-facing host counts, geography, and network concentration for the three named vendors — and does not assess the mitigations above, IOC infrastructure, or attribution.
Rockwell/Allen-Bradley Ethernet/IP
Censys ARC identified 4,148 Internet-exposed hosts that respond to EtherNet/IP and self-identify as Rockwell Automation/Allen-Bradley. The United States remains dominant at 71.0% (2,945 hosts), with Canada a clear second at 11.5% (476 hosts).
Geographic Distribution
Network/ASN Distribution
Combined cellular carriers (Verizon Business, AT&T Mobility, T-Mobile USA) account for 59.0% of all exposed hosts.
Siemens Simatic S7-1200
Censys ARC identified 4,117 Internet-exposed hosts that fingerprint as Siemens SIMATIC S7-1200. Exposure concentrates heavily in southern and central Europe: Greece, Spain, Italy, and Austria together account for 86.0% of the total, each dominated by that country’s leading mobile carrier rather than fixed-line or hosting providers.
Geographic Distribution
Network / ASN Distribution
Schneider Electric (Vendor-Wide)
2,072 internet-exposed hosts fingerprint as Schneider Electric hardware (snapshot 2026-07-30). This query has no PLC-model or protocol filter. This total should not be read as Schneider Electric PLC exposure specifically. Turkey and Australia account for 55.5% of the total combined.
Geographic Distribution
Network/ASN Distribution
Censys Queries
Rockwell/Allen-Bradley:
(host.services.protocol=EIP) and host.services.eip.identity.vendor_name="Rockwell Automation/Allen-Bradley"
Siemens SIMATIC S7-1200:
host.hardware.vendor: "siemens" and host.hardware.product: "simatic_s7-1200"
Schneider Electric:
host.hardware.vendor = "schneider-electric"
results.summary:
CISA has issued an urgent warning regarding threat actors targeting internet-exposed programmable logic controllers in the water sector, leading to operational disruptions and mandatory boil-water notices nationwide.

### Key Points
- Threat actors are locking out operators by changing passwords and disconnecting devices by modifying IP addresses on critical water infrastructure.
- CISA identified Rockwell Automation, Siemens, and Schneider Electric equipment as primary targets for these malicious cyber activities.
- Cellular modems are frequently overlooked in security scans, creating significant blind spots for critical infrastructure operators and system integrators.
- Censys data from July 30, 2026, reveals over 10,000 internet-exposed hosts across the three identified vendors globally.
- Recommended mitigations include removing PLCs from the public internet and routing all remote access through secure VPNs or gateway devices.

### Why it Matters
The targeting of water and wastewater systems poses a direct threat to public health and the reliability of essential utility services. By securing operational technology, organizations can prevent unauthorized access that leads to service outages and dangerous water quality issues.

results.title: You could be taking way better photos on your phone
results.author: David Imel
results.content:
Your smartphone photos can look way better. If you’re willing to put in a little extra work, use third party apps and spend a bit of time editing, it’s possible to take photos that — under the right circumstances — can rival dedicated digital cameras.
You could be taking way better photos on your phone
It takes a little more work, but phones can now legitimately rival point and shoot cameras.
I post a lot of smartphone photos online, and “How do I take better photos on my phone?” is a question I get practically every day. It makes sense. As the saying goes, “The best camera is the one you have on you,” and we practically always have our phones on us these days.
Over the last few years, smartphone camera sensors have gotten bigger, with better light gathering capabilities and higher resolutions. But even though the sensors have gotten bigger and better, the straight-out-of-camera quality through default camera apps hasn’t improved much, if at all. In some respects, smartphone photos have actually gotten worse — aesthetically, at least.
The reason driving this is what people generally use their smartphone cameras for. Smartphone cameras are mostly optimized for information transfer — sending photos of menus, signs, faces and objects that are clear and easy to see. This means phones will usually pull down highlights and pull up the shadows, creating a flatter image that makes it easier to see more information in the frame. But showing more information does not automatically make a photo better. In fact, much of our perception of aesthetics in a photo has to do with its ability to present depth. A photo with too much information in the shadows and highlights will appear washed out. Phones also introduce artifacts like over-sharpening and noise reduction to compensate for their small sensors, which further contributes to the “muddy” smartphone camera look you’re used to seeing by now. This is less necessary now, but many smartphones still do it.
But that doesn’t mean phone cameras are bad. The sensors in modern smartphones have actually gotten so good, many of them can rival dedicated point-and-shoot options on the market today. Knowing how to utilize those sensors is the part most people don’t know how to do, and it really comes down to utilizing some third-party camera and editing apps.
The apps
There are plenty of apps available today that will give you an instantly “aesthetic” photo. Apps like Dazzcam and Hujicam try to emulate film aesthetics like light leaks and polaroid borders (and honestly, if that’s what you’re looking for, they do a fantastic job). There are also apps like Moment Pro Camera II and Halide that offer “Natural” and “Process Zero” modes, which apply far lighter processing than the default camera offers.
Those options are great if you want your pictures to look better instantly without needing to do any additional editing, but if you want the best possible photo, you’ll need to shoot RAW or DNG.
RAW files are a bundle of practically all the information your camera collects, with extremely minimal processing. In most cases, RAW photos won’t necessarily look better than photos straight from the default camera app right away, but that’s because the default camera app makes a lot of creative decisions for you. If you want the highest-quality photo, it’s best to make these creative decisions yourself.
There are tons of apps available that let you shoot RAW, but the apps I use frequently and that I recommend to other people are Moment Pro Camera II and Halide on iOS, and VWFNDR and Zerocam on Android.
I wouldn’t recommend shooting RAW on every photo you take on your phone. Your phone camera is, after all, optimized for what you are probably taking photos of every day. I generally shoot RAW when I see a nice landscape or city scene that I want to share, or if I’m trying to take a portrait of someone and don’t want all the automatic computational phone processing to apply. Really, I shoot RAW when I’m trying to take a photo for artistic purposes, not for informational purposes.
When you’re shooting, you’ll want to tap on your subject in the viewfinder to get the best possible exposure for it. If the rest of the image is a little bright, or a little dark, don’t worry too much. RAW photos retain a lot of information. I should note, though, that under extremely dark circumstances, RAW on smartphones won’t always be the best option. Physics is still physics, and sometimes it’s better to use the computational photography capabilities your phone offers, which mostly shine in low-light environments by stacking multiple frames to reduce noise.
You’ll notice that when you shoot in RAW, the apps will force you to stick to the native focal lengths your phone offers. That’s because RAW images are information straight off the sensor, and cropping applies processing. Photos from the main sensor will often be the best quality, since it usually has the biggest sensor on your phone, so I recommend shooting with it if you can. I do often shoot with the telephoto lens while traveling though, because sometimes you want a little more reach or a little more compression, and you can usually get good photos from that lens as well.
Editing
After you take your photos, you’re going to need to edit them. Most phones won’t show RAW images in the camera gallery, so in order to get them in an editing app, it’s best to use the share sheet and share directly to your editing app of choice. I suggest Snapseed, since it’s totally free and recently got a wonderful visual overhaul. If you’re an Adobe subscriber, Lightroom Mobile is also great, especially if you’re already used to Lightroom’s tools on your computer.
RAW photos don’t usually look great right away, and the magic of RAW is just how much you can tweak the files. Once I have the photo imported, I usually hit the auto button, just to see what the general boundaries are for the image. Auto mode tries to make everything a mid-tone, meaning it will pull down the highlights and pull up the shadows. This will already look better than straight-out-of-camera from your phone’s default camera app, because it isn’t applying noise reduction or sharpening, just highlight, shadow, contrast, and saturation tweaks, but it usually still needs more, or different, adjustments.
Once I see what auto mode wants to do, I’ll either edit from there, or hit the back button and edit myself. A good photo has a natural amount of contrast, with relatively deep shadows and bright highlights. You usually don’t want to go too hard on either of these things, and having a little bit of detail in both of these is usually preferred, but honestly, this is subjective. Occasionally, it’s preferable to crush the highlights and shadows completely, if you’re going for an ultra high-contrast look.
For color, RAW images are usually flatter than most people find pleasing, and you can fix this with either the saturation or vibrance sliders. I generally prefer vibrance. Saturation will increase the saturation of all colors in the image linearly, where vibrance is weighted, increasing saturation of flatter colors more than already-saturated colors. You can overdo this pretty easily, so I recommend having a light touch when it comes to saturation. You can also use white balance to color your image, and many people find a warmer white balance more pleasing, especially when taking photos outside.
Another color tool I love to use is the color mix, or selective editing tool. This allows you to tap on a portion of the image and change some of its values. In Snapseed, you can change the brightness, contrast, saturation, and structure. If you’re in Lightroom mobile, you’ll have access to selective hue shifts, which I use all the time. This allows you to shift a yellow tone towards more orange or green, or shift a blue tone more cyan or purple.
Most editing apps also include geometry or perspective tools. These tools allow you to adjust distortion, aspect, scale, and offset. If you don’t know what that means, try hitting the auto button in the geometry or perspective setting. You might be surprised how distorted your phone captured a scene compared to what it looks like in reality, but this is image-dependent. If you want to straighten lines in your photo, some editing apps offer a guided tool that allows you to manually add guidance lines to tell the program what lines should be straight in the image.
The tools you’ll want to use are going to depend heavily on what you want the image to convey. For example, when I’m doing architectural photography, I rely a lot more heavily on the perspective tools, because the aesthetic of the image is heavily dictated by its geometry. If I’m photographing a landscape, I’m more focused on tone and color. Not every scene needs to be tweaked with every tool, and how you edit comes down to personal taste. That taste can also take a while to develop, so study the photos you like and try to figure out how they were edited.
When you’re done with your edits, many editing apps like Snapseed and Lightroom Mobile also come with a handy tool to put a matte (or border) around your image. I think that photos look better with a white border, as it isolates the image for your eyes. You obviously don’t have to use this tool, but I really like it. Have some whimsy!
This process is a lot more work than just opening your camera app and snapping, but the results are worth it. I am continuously blown away by the quality of images I’m able to get off smartphones, and just how close they can be to a dedicated camera. If you don’t believe me, check out this video I did comparing RAW photos from the iPhone 17 Pro to the Leica M11.
Photography by David Imel / The Verge

Smartphone users can achieve professional-grade photography by utilizing third-party apps to capture RAW files and applying manual editing techniques to bypass default, over-processed computational camera settings.

### Key Points
- Default smartphone cameras prioritize information clarity, often resulting in flat, over-sharpened, or "muddy" images due to aggressive computational processing.
- Shooting in RAW or DNG formats preserves original sensor data, allowing for greater creative control during the post-processing stage.
- Recommended third-party camera apps include Moment Pro Camera II and Halide for iOS, and VWFNDR and Zerocam for Android.
- Editing tools like Snapseed and Adobe Lightroom Mobile enable users to adjust contrast, vibrance, white balance, and perspective to enhance image aesthetics.
- RAW photography is best suited for artistic landscapes or portraits, while default camera modes remain superior for low-light environments using frame-stacking technology.

### Why it Matters
Moving beyond default camera settings allows users to unlock the full potential of modern smartphone sensors, which now rival dedicated point-and-shoot cameras. Mastering these manual workflows shifts the focus from simple information capture to intentional, high-quality artistic photography.

results.title: Windows Hello vs. Enhanced Sign‑in Security: Which sign‑in method actually keeps your Windows 11 PC safer, and what's the difference?
results.author: mhuck@live.com (Mauro Huculak) , Mauro Huculak
results.content:
Microsoft is expanding one of the least understood security features in Windows 11. Beginning with the August 2026 update, Enhanced Sign-in Security (ESS) now supports compatible external fingerprint readers, extending the company's most secure Windows Hello experience to devices without built-in biometric hardware.
The timing couldn't be better because Enhanced Sign-in Security has confused users ever since Microsoft introduced it. Some users assume it's simply a newer version of Windows Hello, while others think it's reserved for businesses or Copilot+ PCs.
The reality is that Windows Hello and Windows Hello Enhanced Sign-in Security use the same sign-in experience, but they protect your biometric data in different ways.
After spending time digging through Microsoft's support page, I think that's the distinction most explanations miss. Enhanced Sign-in Security isn't about making facial recognition more accurate or fingerprint sign-in faster. It's about making the entire authentication process harder to attack.
Standard Windows Hello is already one of the best security features
Before the Enhanced Sign-in Security feature was introduced, Windows Hello had already replaced passwords with a much stronger authentication model.
Instead of storing passwords that can be stolen or reused, Windows Hello creates cryptographic credentials that are attached to the Trusted Platform Module (TPM) available on your computer. Facial recognition and fingerprints are used only to unlock those credentials, and your biometric templates remain on the device rather than being uploaded to Microsoft's servers.
For the average home user, that already provides excellent protection against phishing, password reuse, and stolen credentials.
The Enhanced Sign-in Security feature doesn't replace the architecture already in place. Instead, it builds another layer on top of it.
The real difference is where the trust is placed
This is where the comparison becomes interesting. Using the standard Windows Hello, the operating system relies on the system to process biometric authentication after receiving data from the trusted sensor. Enhanced Sign-in Security moves much of that work into isolated, hardware-protected environments.
When using the Enhanced Sign-in Security feature, Microsoft improves that trust. Instead of allowing sensitive biometric operations to occur in the normal Windows environment, the feature isolates them using Virtualization-Based Security (VBS) and Trusted Platform Module (TPM) 2.0 technology.
The algorithms for facial recognition run in a protected memory region, secure fingerprint readers perform matching within the hardware itself, and communication between the biometric sensor and the operating system is encrypted and isolated.
In other words, Windows Hello protects your credentials, and Windows Hello Enhanced Sign-in Security protects both your credentials and the path your biometric data takes before Windows 11 authenticates you.
Fingerprints show the biggest difference
The August 2026 Security Update highlights the biggest architectural difference between standard Windows Hello and Enhanced Sign-in Security.
Using a standard Windows Hello fingerprint reader, the sensor captures your fingerprint, and Windows 11 verifies it securely using the operating system and TPM-backed credentials.
An ESS-compatible fingerprint reader moves more of that process into the hardware itself. These readers include a dedicated secure processor, store fingerprint templates inside the device, contain a Microsoft-issued certificate that proves they're trusted hardware, and establish an encrypted communication channel with the operating system. Instead of receiving raw biometric data, Windows 11 receives only the authentication result.
Microsoft hasn't explained why ESS still doesn't support external Windows Hello cameras (likely because USB can be a vector for attack). However, its support page shows that enhanced security for facial recognition relies on specific camera hardware, firmware, and protected memory through Virtualization-Based Security (VBS), whereas ESS fingerprint readers can perform biometric matching inside certified hardware. That architectural difference may explain why Microsoft expanded support for external fingerprint readers first.
The practical benefit is a smaller attack surface. In simple terms, even if malware gains elevated privileges, it has fewer ways to interfere with the biometric authentication process.
Should you enable Enhanced Sign-in Security?
If your computer doesn't support Enhanced Sign-in Security, there's no reason to worry. The standard security of Windows Hello remains one of the strongest consumer authentication systems available, and it's already a significant upgrade over passwords.
However, if your device includes Enhanced Sign-in Security-compatible hardware, or you're planning to buy a new external fingerprint reader that supports the feature, I'd recommend enabling it and leaving it on.
Not because Windows Hello suddenly became insecure, but because the enhanced option can add an extra layer of security. If your hardware supports it, there's little downside to leaving it enabled.
How to enable the enhanced security feature
If the feature is available for your Windows Hello-compatible authentication device, you can enable it by going to Settings > Accounts > Sign-in options.
Once the USB fingerprint reader is connected and recognized by the operating system, on this page, under the "Additional settings" section, check the state of the "Enhanced sign-in security" setting.
If your system wasn't previously running ESS, you may see a prompt showing "Pending set up" or "Update PIN."
If the "Update PIN" option shows up, use it to complete the setup. On the other hand, if you see the "Pending set up" option, then configure the "Fingerprint recognition" feature under the "Ways to sign in" section.
One important note. When upgrading your system to Enhanced Sign-in Security, Windows 11 will remove any existing non-ESS biometric enrollments and associated credentials to ensure a clean, secure environment. You will need to refresh your PIN and register your fingerprints again using the new sensor. Once complete, the ESS toggle will show as enabled.
Also, while the feature is turned on, you won't be able to use peripherals that do not support the security feature.
Windows Central's Take
Microsoft hasn't done itself any favors with the name "Enhanced Sign-in Security." It sounds like an entirely new authentication system, when in reality it's an evolution of Windows Hello that strengthens how biometric authentication is processed behind the scenes. A lot of users will never notice the difference because the sign-in experience is exactly the same.
What makes the August 2026 Security Update important isn't that Windows Hello suddenly became more secure, as the standard Windows Hello has long been one of the strongest authentication systems available on consumer devices. The real significance is that the company is lifting the limitations by adding support for compatible external fingerprint readers.
If your computer already supports Enhanced Sign-in Security, I'd leave it enabled. If it doesn't, I wouldn't replace perfectly good hardware to get the feature because standard Windows Hello is already an excellent authentication system. However, if you're buying a new fingerprint reader for your computer, choosing an Enhanced Sign-in Security-compatible model is the better long-term investment since Microsoft is clearly expanding support for that ecosystem.
Do you think Enhanced Sign-in Security is worth using, or is standard Windows Hello already enough for your needs? Let me know in the comments.

Microsoft is expanding its Enhanced Sign-in Security feature in the August 2026 Windows 11 update to include support for compatible external fingerprint readers for improved biometric authentication.

### Key Points
- Enhanced Sign-in Security (ESS) isolates biometric processing using Virtualization-Based Security (VBS) and TPM 2.0 technology.
- The update allows external fingerprint readers with dedicated secure processors to perform matching within the hardware itself.
- ESS creates an encrypted communication channel between the biometric sensor and the operating system to reduce the potential attack surface.
